title: Trevor Quick on Harvey.ai as the Utility Belt for Lawyers
author: Trevor Quick

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Quick does not adopt the cluster’s competence-crisis framing. He redirects attention from the loss of apprenticeship work toward augmentation, professional fulfilment and earlier focus on difficult problems, claiming AI can support lawyer development while routine work is completed. However, he provides no concrete replacement training model or evidence that this preserves independent expertise and verification ability.
qs: So I think in a profession that really does struggle with how do you train attorneys to get better without just giving them the work,  Harvey offers a lot of ways that you can use it and get that work done while actually feeling a little bit more like you’re growing as a person and growing as an attorney.
Ultimately, I think that the success we’re having is due to people really buying into the idea that AI augments their capabilities.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source indicates that clients’ generative-AI adoption pressures law firms to keep pace and reports anecdotal time savings, but it does not address whether corporate legal departments will selectively insource work or reduce outside-counsel instructions. Its implications for the cluster’s principal proposition therefore remain indeterminate.
qs: If your clients are undergoing this kind of generative AI revolution that we’re seeing globally in every facet of our lives, and you as a law firm are not going along with them, can be a hard conversation.
But also, I know you’ve heard this because I’ve heard this, when people use something and they see that something that took hours to do can now take minutes to do.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source contains only closing remarks and no substantive claims about legal AI, organisational adaptation, human control, employment, pricing or adoption. There is therefore insufficient evidence to assess its position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source aligns with the shift toward informed procurement by presenting a market-data tool for targeted comparison of legal technologies and source-linked verification. This materially adds a procurement-information mechanism, while offering no measured evidence that either Navigator or Harvey produces sustained adoption, performance or economic value.
qs: And we’ve built a generative AI bot that sits on GPT 4.0 and is grounded in our LTH data so that users, in addition to browsing and keyword searching, can now come to the site and ask very targeted questions like,  is Definely SOC 2 certified?

Answers will be generated along with links to the relevant sources on the site so you can verify answers and focus your research and reading and access the deep analytical content on our site more easily.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source accepts the need for disciplined market research and materially extends it by presenting LTH Navigator as a natural-language interface for workflow-specific vendor comparison, security and hosting questions, with source links enabling verification. Harvey’s funding and LexisNexis integration further illustrate market expansion, though their effects remain unproven.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Quick accepts the human-led, selectively deployed workflow framing and adds a concrete implementation: integrating authoritative Lexis sources and citation signals directly into Harvey to make research outputs easier to access and verify. His emphasis on optional adoption, reduced interface friction and cautious forecasting reinforces operating-model and interaction-design priorities, though it does not establish broader capability, productivity or labour-market effects.
qs: that case law, that statutory law, those shepherd citations in a format that’s very intuitive and easy for them to access, as well as verify very quickly so that they continue to benefit from the efficiencies of generative AI powered by Harvey.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: Quick supports the cluster’s augmentation account: Harvey can remove rote legal tasks, refocus lawyers on higher-value problems and potentially aid professional development. His evidence is experiential and does not address the broader claims about agentic infrastructure, vendor durability, pricing or employment outcomes.
qs: And Harvey allows them to re-center on the work that actually feels and rewards what they want to do, those difficult problems.

So I think in a profession that really does struggle with how do you train attorneys to get better without just giving them the work,  Harvey offers a lot of ways that you can use it and get that work done while actually feeling a little bit more like you’re growing as a person and growing as an attorney.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that client-side adoption and competitive pressure are important drivers of law-firm AI adoption, while technical quality and security are prerequisites for a credible offering. Its claims are largely analogical, anecdotal and provider-reported, consistent with the cluster’s caution that market-wide evidence remains early; it does not materially address pricing reform, apprenticeship or end-to-end delivery redesign.
qs: If your clients are undergoing this kind of generative AI revolution that we’re seeing globally in every facet of our lives, and you as a law firm are not going along with them, can be a hard conversation.

I think that’s where, again, having subject matter experts, being honest and being so innovative allows us to step in and say, hey, we can be a great solution for you, but we can also be the type of solution you can talk to your clients about and they’re not gonna have concerns because we put the technical side at the forefront, the security side at the forefront.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Quick supports the cluster’s framing of AI as augmenting lawyers and shifting them away from routine production rather than simply replacing them. He also recognises the profession’s work-based training problem and claims Harvey can pair task completion with professional growth, though he provides no measured evidence or concrete succession-pipeline design.
qs: Ultimately, I think that the success we’re having is due to people really buying into the idea that AI augments their capabilities.

So I think in a profession that really does struggle with how do you train attorneys to get better without just giving them the work,  Harvey offers a lot of ways that you can use it and get that work done while actually feeling a little bit more like you’re growing as a person and growing as an attorney.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: Quick supports the cluster’s proposition by linking Harvey’s large-firm-first strategy to quality signalling and by presenting integrations, legal expertise and customer-shaped workflows as the basis for becoming embedded infrastructure. His emphasis on candid limitations and lawyer verification also reinforces the governed copilot model, while his growth and performance claims remain company-reported rather than independent proof of accuracy or productivity.
qs: I think one of the interesting things about the way that Winston and Gabe kind of approached Harvey’s growth from the earliest stages is that they wanted to work with the biggest and the best firms and cement the quality market signaling in that way.
But we also know that attorneys want to verify the information they’re getting from Harvey, from any generative AI tool.

st.t: Legal platforms: Content and governance differentiate workflows
st.an: Quick supports the cluster’s core proposition by presenting authoritative-content integration as a way to expand Harvey’s workflow coverage and reduce interface switching, while expressly retaining attorney verification. His unsupported claim of best-in-class testing also aligns with the cluster’s caution that performance evidence is largely vendor-reported.
qs: think making it native to the platform, the one thing that we consistently hear from maybe more skeptical ⁓ prospective partners is, don’t want to make my attorneys, my users kind of jump around to a bunch of different windows to leverage the full capacity of generative AI.
But we also know that attorneys want to verify the information they’re getting from Harvey, from any generative AI tool.

st.an: The source supports the synthesis by framing legal AI adoption as an operational and client-facing proposition grounded in subject-matter expertise, technical quality and security, rather than model capability alone. It also reinforces competitive and client pressure as adoption drivers, while its success and time-saving claims remain anecdotal and unquantified. It does not materially address contextual agents, lawyer supervision or verification.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: Quick supports the proposition that value depends on effective implementation rather than access alone. He describes initial use-case guidance, sustained responsiveness to users and customer-led workflow development, while framing benefits as lawyer augmentation and relief from rote work. His evidence is qualitative and does not establish comparative performance or realised organisational value.
qs: I think what’s really exciting to me about Workflow Builder is the opportunity to partner directly with some of the amazing folks internally, whether again at law firms or in-house that we partner with already to ideate and really kind of scheme up how they can use this tool most effectively.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that legal-AI value depends on organisational and client-facing absorption rather than access alone. Quick identifies client pressure, subject-matter expertise, technical quality and security as adoption drivers, while the historical analogy and unmeasured success claims remain anecdotal and do not establish broader productivity or business-model effects.

st.an: Quick supports the cluster’s core proposition by framing Harvey as augmenting lawyers while removing repetitive, time-intensive production work and allowing greater focus on difficult legal problems. He also supports client-driven adoption pressure, but offers mainly personal and promotional evidence rather than measured effects on employment, pricing or service-delivery structures.

Ultimately, I think that the success we’re having is due to people really buying into the idea that AI augments their capabilities.

st.an: Quick supports the cluster’s view that legal-AI adoption is driven by competitive strategy, client expectations and trust-related implementation considerations rather than technology alone. His emphasis on subject-matter expertise, technical quality and security aligns with multidisciplinary, client-focused service redesign, although his evidence is analogical and self-reported rather than measured.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Quick supports the cluster’s central augmentation account: Harvey removes repetitive legal tasks while complementing lawyers and redirecting them toward more rewarding work. His claims are practitioner-based and do not resolve the cluster’s uncertainty about staffing, employment, verification, or measured productivity outcomes.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: Quick supports the cluster’s qualified view by presenting funding and adoption as signs of market recognition while grounding Harvey’s appeal in legal expertise and guided implementation. kp.k: Funding and partnerships support Harvey’s platform expansion
kp.d: Lambert reports a $300 million Series E funding round and $5 billion valuation. Quick interprets the funding as recognition of Harvey’s growth and a means to extend it, rather than claiming knowledge of investors’ motives. He argues that relationships with technical, financial and legal-information institutions confer credibility with scrutinising legal buyers and support further partnerships.
qs: So $300 million series e-funding and a $5 billion valuation.
You know, I’m not sure what investors are thinking, but I’ll say what I think, you know, our users and our partner firms and our partner in-house teams really resonate with.
And partnering with those institutions really helps give us credibility on every front.

kp.k: Embedded legal expertise underpins adoption and product deployment
kp.d: Quick attributes customer engagement to combining generative AI expertise with practitioners who understand legal use cases. His team of attorneys supporting go-to-market sales grew from his being the first person in January of the preceding year to approaching 30 people in 18 months. He also reports that a recent Fortune article put attorneys at 18 percent of Harvey’s workforce. These are reported staffing figures and his explanation of adoption, not a measured causal finding.
qs: I was the first person in seat in January last year for my team, a team of attorneys who partner with our GTM sales leads to really make sure that potential users understand what Harvey can do and how it can do it so effectively.
And that team is now approaching 30 people.
A recent Fortune article kind of, I think, pegged at 18 percent of the company are attorneys.

kp.k: Lexis integration extends Harvey into native legal research
kp.d: Lambert contrasts existing advice to use Harvey with supplied data, rather than for pure legal research, with the proposed Lexis capability; Quick confirms that distinction. Quick describes an optional add-on bringing US case law, statutory law and Shepard citations into Harvey, reducing movement between systems. He frames this as the first step in a potentially broader partnership, with US materials to be brought up and running.
qs: It is an add-on, and so if folks aren’t interested, they are welcome to say that they’re fine with Harvey as is, and that’s a lot of people,
So the same way that they would want to use and leverage generative AI to kind of dissect legal research across that database, they’re doing now native in the Harvey platform

So I think step one is getting that case law, that statutory law, those Shepard citations for the US up and running, and then figuring out where else we can deploy their kind of expertise and data set with our generative AI know-how.

kp.k: Source visibility supports human verification of AI outputs
kp.d: Quick distinguishes testing Harvey’s outputs from attorneys checking information before relying on it. He claims internal and external testing produces best-in-class marks, but supplies no study design or numerical results. The stated verification mechanism is direct access to legal authorities and citations through Lexis, intended to preserve efficiency while allowing lawyers to check outputs.
qs: And we’ve always been big on trust but verify.
We internally and externally test Harvey’s outputs and we really are very excited that we have those best-in-class marks when kind of tested in that way.
But we also know that attorneys want to verify the information they’re getting from Harvey, from any generative AI tool.

kp.k: Document integrations aim to embed AI in existing work
kp.d: Quick presents the Microsoft Word add-in, existing SharePoint and Google Drive integrations, and planned comprehensive iManage integration as a strategy of meeting attorneys within their current workflows. He anticipates making documents held in iManage more accessible and valuable and connecting the companies’ user bases. His assertion of an exclusive official partnership position is a vendor claim.
qs: That’s why we have a Microsoft Word add-in. That’s why we already have integrations with SharePoint and Google Drive, and we’re excited to add iManage to that.
But the integration will be comprehensive.
And we are the only legal tech generative AI company out there that has an official partnership with iManage.

kp.k: Custom workflows give customers greater control over legal automation
kp.d: Quick describes Workflow Builder as moving from standardised agentic workflows toward low-code and no-code customer-built solutions, recognising firms’ and in-house teams’ knowledge of how they want work performed. He describes Vault enhancements as improving bulk review and allowing users to contribute their legal thinking to outputs, while deep research mode expands agent workflows for complex legal work. These are capability claims, not quantified productivity findings.
qs: into an industry first series of low code, no code, self-build custom solutions.

We always recognize that we are working with some of the foremost legal minds and legal businesses in the world, and we have the humility to recognize that they understand better how they wanna do things

And this will allow them to better engage in those bulk document reviews more efficiently and effectively, while also allowing them to better input their own legal thoughts into the output that Harvey provides.
And then for deep research mode, think just really enabling legal agent workflows across more and more capabilities that meet the most complex legal workflows that our users are engaging with.

kp.k: Use patterns differ across firms and in-house teams
kp.d: Asked which new feature is gaining adoption fastest, Quick offers no comparative adoption figures or measured success story. He instead describes differing customer use patterns, including firms particularly committed to Vault, and calls Harvey a utility belt used in different ways. He also claims rapid transfer of foundational-model improvements into the product.
qs: I mean, think really per usual with Harvey’s functionalities, it depends on the firm.
We continue to be that utility belt that firms use in different ways or in-house teams as well.
we have firms that really just are all in on Vault
the speed with which we were able to take it from open AI announces it to we’re deploying it

kp.k: Knowledge management and innovation teams help shape development
kp.d: Quick describes customer knowledge management and innovation professionals as collaborators who connect Harvey with attorneys and legal-adjacent users and inform its roadmap. He says product conversations are bilateral and include feedback from organisations that do not ultimately buy Harvey. Workflow Builder is presented as a way to extend these professionals’ existing work.
qs: Whether those are folks who kind of decide to go with us or not. It’s valuable all the same
our product team is constantly on calls not just previewing the roadmap not dictating but as is true of everything we try to do across the platform really making sure it’s a bilateral conversation
like I think with Workflow Builder, really elevate what they’re already doing

kp.k: Adoption combines candour, capacity growth and peer signalling
kp.d: Lambert reports having read that one-third of the AmLaw 100 uses Harvey rather than merely piloting it. Quick attributes adoption to practitioner support, candour about technological limitations, security and peer influence. He reports document-handling capacity rising from five documents to 10,000 in Vault during his 18 months at Harvey, with the change taking approximately a year. His analogy to firms following Skadden into hostile-takeover work explains the proposed competitive imitation mechanism; it is not evidence measuring AI adoption.
qs: a third of the AmLaw 100
These are areas where you might run into more issues that are endemic to the technology.
In my time at Harvey, we’ve gone from being able to handle five documents at a time to now 10,000 in vault.
And that’s in now 18 months, but I think that that took place in about a year.

If your clients are undergoing this kind of generative AI revolution that we’re seeing globally in every facet of our lives, and you as a law firm are not going along with them, can be a hard conversation.

kp.k: Quick frames task automation as augmentation, not job elimination
kp.d: Lambert raises lawyers’ fears of job loss when hours of work become minutes. Quick responds with his reported experience of attorneys welcoming relief from repetitive tasks, using documentary diligence as an example. He argues that Harvey redirects attention toward difficult problems, professional growth and client advocacy in firms and in-house departments. This is an augmentation argument grounded in personal experience and customer conversations, not evidence of employment effects or a demonstrated replacement for training through work.
qs: what I hear from attorneys that I speak with every day is excitement for what it’s going to eliminate off of their plate every day.
We’re talking about bulk rote tasks that take hours and hours on end.
So I think in a profession that really does struggle with how do you train attorneys to get better without just giving them the work,
Ultimately, I think that the success we’re having is due to people really buying into the idea that AI augments their capabilities.

kp.k: Expansion reaches adjacent professions and law-firm business functions
kp.d: Asked about tax, accounting and compliance, Quick proposes extending Harvey’s legal-market strategy through leading organisations, industry-specific expertise and adaptable use cases. He cites already working with PWC and interest from firms and in-house teams. Separately, he confirms use in marketing, client alerts and legal-adjacent workflows; these descriptions contain no adoption volumes or measured outcomes.
qs: they wanted to work with the biggest and the best firms and cement the quality market signaling in that way.
We want to have expertise on our end that’s not just generative AI, but is specific to those industries and those use cases
Ultimately, I think already working with PWC, seeing a lot of interest with in-house teams, with law firms about different applications and practice areas of Harvey.
You never thought you could get me so excited about client alerts and marketing stuff for someone who did not choose to do that path.

kp.k: Future vision emphasises usability, collaboration and broader legal access
kp.d: Quick explicitly qualifies his ability to predict the future, then anticipates more intuitive interfaces, reduced prompting and window-switching burdens, and secure collaboration between law firms and in-house clients. He also states an aspiration to democratise access to the legal system, but offers no specific mechanism or evidence of reduced unmet legal need.
qs: if I try to predict the future, I’m going to remove all doubt about my lack of knowledge about the future.
whether it’s prompting burden or kind of window jumping as we were talking about, I think the other thing is collaboration.
We’re hearing a tremendous amount of appetite both from the law firm side as well as from the kind of in-house or client side that they want to be working together.
Ultimately, I think we really want to move towards just democratizing access to the legal system.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Quick presents Harvey as an integrated utility belt that expands the steps lawyers can perform with AI, including legal research and document access.
pts.d: Trevor Quick says the LexisNexis partnership enables research within Harvey using case law, statutory law and Shepard citations, reducing movement between systems and making human verification easier. He describes the forthcoming iManage integration as making existing documents more accessible and valuable. These are claims about integrating and augmenting lawyers' workflows, not eliminating verification.

pts.k: Quick says custom workflows, bulk review improvements and deep research extend AI into more complex, user-directed legal work.
pts.d: Quick characterises Workflow Builder as a transition from standardised agentic workflows to low-code/no-code custom solutions. He says Vault improvements enable more efficient bulk document review while incorporating users' legal thinking, and that deep research extends legal agent workflows to more complex tasks. He also expects these capabilities to elevate the work of innovation and knowledge-management teams.

pts.k: Quick frames AI as augmenting lawyers by removing rote work and allowing greater concentration on difficult problems and client advocacy.
pts.d: Responding to concerns about job elimination, Quick emphasises relief from time-consuming diligence and other bulk tasks, improved professional satisfaction and greater effectiveness. He suggests lawyers can complete work while developing professionally. He does not provide a quantified employment forecast or explicitly demonstrate that displacement cannot occur.

pts.k: Quick links adoption to legal expertise, candid implementation support, institutional credibility and pressure to keep pace with clients.
pts.d: Quick argues that combining technical development with practising-lawyer expertise helps users identify applications and makes the product stickier. He presents investor and partner relationships as credibility signals. Drawing an analogy with law-firm imitation of successful competitors, he suggests firms face difficult client conversations if they do not participate in clients' adoption of generative AI. These are his explanations of adoption rather than measured causal findings.

pts.k: Quick anticipates broader professional-service applications, more intuitive interfaces and secure collaboration between firms and clients.
pts.d: Quick describes expansion into adjacent professional services through industry-specific expertise and partnerships with leading organisations. He reports existing use in marketing and client alerts. His longer-term vision includes reduced prompting and system-switching burdens and secure collaboration between law firms and in-house teams. Democratizing access to the legal system is stated as an aspiration, without a specific mechanism or evidence of reduced unmet civil legal need.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Quick's company experience, user feedback and descriptions of product capabilities; performance testing is asserted without results.
pts.d: Quick speaks as Harvey's strategic business-development representative and a former transactional attorney. He invokes daily conversations with attorneys, partnerships with firms and in-house teams, product-team feedback and his own diligence experience. He says internal and external tests produce best-in-class marks, but supplies no named benchmark, methodology, scores or comparative results. Human verification through citations is described separately from this testing. No measured time savings, client outcomes or employment effects are supplied.

pts.k: Quick offers specific company growth and capacity figures, alongside qualitative accounts of adoption and expansion.
pts.d: Quick reports that his attorney team grew from one person to nearly 30 in 18 months and cites a Fortune article estimating that attorneys comprise 18 percent of Harvey. He reports document capacity rising from five to 10,000 in Vault, with Lambert corroborating the initial five-document limit. These figures concern staffing and processing capacity, not independently measured quality or productivity. Quick also mentions firms heavily using Vault and work with PwC. The host's statement about adoption by a third of the AmLaw 100 is not treated as a figure supplied by Quick.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview distinguishes recent feature releases and rapid capacity growth from staged integrations and undated future ambitions.
pts.d: In this 2025 transcript, Quick says the three highlighted capabilities developed in approximately the preceding month. He places the five-to-10,000-document capacity increase within his 18 months at Harvey, probably occurring over about a year. Lexis research is an optional add-on, with US case law, statutes and Shepard citations the initial integration step. He uses future tense for the comprehensive iManage integration. Broader collaboration, intuitiveness and access aspirations have no firm completion date.

pts.k: Quick qualifies benefits by user needs, responsible deployment and technological limitations, and explicitly cautions against precise forecasting.
pts.d: Quick says adoption varies by firm, stresses that users understand their own workflows, and describes candid guidance about where generative AI may encounter difficulties as necessary to building trust. Continued human verification remains part of the proposed workflow. His future vision is thematic and conditional rather than a confident forecast of a specific legal-market structure.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries described are law-firm and in-house users, their clients, and knowledge-management, innovation and business-support teams.
pts.d: Lawyers gain integrated research, custom workflows and bulk-review support, with transactional diligence a concrete example of rote work to be reduced. Firms and in-house departments use different combinations of capabilities. Innovation and KM teams help shape deployment and product development; marketing and other legal-adjacent users develop additional applications. Clients are said to benefit through more effective advocacy and prospective collaboration. Quick's market strategy emphasises leading firms and professional-service organisations, including PwC; Harvey is presented as the software provider, not an ALSP delivering legal work.
